The Thompson groups are a sequence of groups distinguished by their simplicity and
rich mathematical structure, particularly in their complexity. This paper
investigates four groups related to the Thompson group V, specifically three
generalized versions and one braided variant, analyzing their characteristics
through divergence measurements. If a group has a finite diviser set, it exhibits
uniform finite divergence. The Thompson group F is shown to have finite
divergence with itself, using a 4-diviser set. The 2-Thompson group acts on two
brances of the interval branched line, J, and the F_2 homeomorphisms' action on
J naturally defines a diviser set. The paper proves that the generalized
Thompson groups have finite divergence with each other and with the braided
Thompson group, all using a 5-diviser set. The braided Thompson group V^∞,
involving infinite braiding, has finite divergence with V, using a 6-diviser
set. The paper's conclusions also relate to the braided Thompson group V_2, the 2-Thompson
group's right-acting on J.

Recently, large language models like BERT have achieved great success in various natural language processing tasks. To further improve their performance, more structured approaches such as question-answering have been developed to provide specific context information for LLMs. Specifically, the document-ranking algorithm, RAG, has been designed with a focus on structured data. By fine-tuning RAG for question-answering, it is possible to enhance both the retrieval and extraction of relevant information. In this study, we demonstrate the effectiveness of fine-tuning RAG's complete architecture on question-answering tasks, highlighting the importance of end-to-end fine-tuning of both retrieval and generation components. We also show that pre-training RAG with unstructured data leads to improved performance and more efficient multi-document processing capabilities.

This paper examines the limiting behavior of the Zeros of the Orthopologarithmic Family (OOF) - a set of orthogonal polynomials constructed under a specific logarithmic weight function, $W(x) = \ln(1 + |t-x|^2)$, and weighs the influence of the point $t$ where this function and its derivative vanish. The study begins by establishing two fundamental theorems related to the OOF polynomials: one concerning the limiting empirical distribution of the Zeros and another regarding the rate at which the zeros of the OOF polynomials $L_n(x)$ converge. In the general case, when $W$ is replaced by an arbitrary weight function $w$, the study investigates the limiting behavior of the Zeros using two phase diagram illustrations, one for the logarithmic case and the other for the Hermitian case, under a specific weight matrix $\Gamma = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$.

Crowdsourcing has become a well-established technique for gathering information from numerous individuals. One of the primary crowdsourcing platforms is Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk), which allows researchers to post tasks known as HITs and recruit workers to complete them. Studies utilizing MTurk have generated a substantial amount of valuable data, including those in the fields of psychology and neuroscience. However, finding subjects willing to participate and ensuring their compliance with the study requirements can be a significant challenge. Prior studies have focused on the selection process of MTurk studies, which involve administering qualification tests to filter qualified workers. This paper examines the effectiveness of different qualification processes in achieving this goal, and discovers that the specific tasks used in the tests and the level of approval from study participants can greatly impact the results.

We aim to develop a method for retrieving text segments from long texts that contain query phrases, but current approaches based on transformers are computationally expensive and only partially effective in the task. To address this issue, we propose the Token Shift and Selection network (TS2-Net), a new approach that tokenizes and rearranges as well as selectively extracts text segments based on attention and selection masks. TS2-Net can efficiently identify the text segments most relevant to the query and significantly outperforms the existing state-of-the-art transformer-based retrieval models. Notably, TS2-Net's performance surpasses that of the renowned BERT model, while requiring only 12% of its parameters. TS2-Net's success is enhanced by its ability to capture long-range contextual dependencies, achieved by tokenization with a sliding window and shifting, and to efficiently process the retrieved text segments, achieved by using an encoder-decoder architecture with shared parameters. TS2-Net's tokenization and processing strategies are highly efficient and robust, as demonstrated by the network's strong generalization to out-of-vocabulary multi-sentence queries, and its ability to perform well on various retrieval tasks with a single optimized model.

The top quark's taste, which is a key aspect of its flavor composition, can be explored through flavor-changing neutral currents. If the top's flavor makeup contains an anomalous component, it would give rise to specific, detectable signals in $t\rightarrow ch$ and $t\rightarrow ch^\ast$ decays. We have found a new taste variety that can cause these transitions. This new taste variety can cause changes in flavor when particles interact with neutral currents, potentially making contributions to $t\rightarrow ch$ and $t\rightarrow ch^\ast$ decays. We have calculated the cross sections for the proton-target Drell-Yan process, which could detect these decays with appropriate experimental conditions and could reveal the top's taste variety through observation of $t\rightarrow ch$ and $t\rightarrow ch^\ast$ decays if they are produced at a certain rate of 5 ab$^{-1}$ at the FCC-hh collider.

We explore new models of hybrid growing networks that integrate elements of preferential attachment and uniform attachment, building upon existing research in this field. We focus on developing algorithms to calculate key statistical properties of these networks, such as their degree distribution, average degree, and behavior observed through two-dimensional probability plots. We also investigate the evolution of these networks over time, examining their average size, average degree, and other characteristics at different stages of growth. Our numerical results validate our algorithms and provide a comprehensive understanding of these networks' behavior as they grow. We also use theoretical models to explain our findings and offer general guidance for modeling real-world networks that display unique characteristics.

The rapid growth in wireless communication technology has led to increased interference from adjacent services, thereby making it crucial to accurately predict these interferences. This interference prediction, a critical function in shared wireless communication systems, aids in optimizing performance, particularly for critical applications such as healthcare, vehicle-to-everything communication, and remote surgery. Existing literature has primarily focused on single-label interference prediction; however, environments where multiple services coexist simultaneously generates multiple types of interferences, thus rendering single-label interference prediction insufficient for practical applications. This paper presents a novel approach to address multi-label interference prediction by training convolutional neural networks on theoretical propagation data. The non-relativistic KG equation solutions in cosmic string spacetime featuring an interstellar dislocation are examined. The wave functions and corresponding energies of KG particles are derived for model parameters $\beta = 2$ and $\lambda = 1$, with calculations performed via the Hamilton-Jacobi method. The analyses reveal that matter waves coexist with dislocations, forming correlations similar to those found in fractals, and that the dislocation impacts the energies of KG particles. Furthermore, the formation of a spin-dependent energy band due to dislocation is observed, with its width decreasing as the dislocation diminishes. The research demonstrates that the dislocation gives rise to correlations between energy and charge, an effect absent in uniform spacetime.

In the theory of measure algebras, a significant role is played by
$\sigma$-complete locally compact measure algebras, which can be regarded as
the algebraic counterpart to locally compact groups.  Measure algebras that
are locally compact but not compact are relatively isolated in the broader
category of measure algebras.  Every locally compact measure algebra that
is not a group has a compact embedding from its group model, a measure
algebra that is naturally associated with it.  This paper presents a
characterization of locally compact measure algebras that are isomorphically
similar to compact ones, under conditions of separability.  Specifically, a
measure algebra is locally compact and separable and resembles a compact
one if and only if it is compactly embedded into the algebra of its continuous
homomorphisms, which is also locally compact.

In our study, we investigate the recoil proton polarization resulting from deep virtual Compton scattering on the nucleus. This polarization is generated by the spatial separation of charge and magnetization of the virtual Compton amplitude in the final state. Our analysis reveals that the recoil proton polarization is capable of distinguishing between different quantum corrections arising from photon exchange. This polarization offers considerable advantages in the following aspects: it can be measured with ease using a single polarized target, is not affected by higher-order radiation corrections, and complements the existing DVCS observables. Notably, the recoiling proton polarization offers unique insights into the electromagnetic form factors of the nucleon, the generalized parton distributions, and the gluon form factor, which cannot be determined through traditional CLAS measurements.

The advent of synthetic intelligence has sparked debate about its future development, with some envisioning superintelligence far beyond present human capabilities. However, achieving such advancements might prove impossible without augmenting synthetic intelligence using techniques inspired by human augmentation. Focusing on computational augmented synthetic intelligence, this research defines key characteristics, discusses underlying technologies, and outlines benefits and challenges. Evaluating computational CSAI processes two fundamental properties - efficiency and reliability. As a pioneering field, green augmented synthetic intelligence is proposed, incorporating ecological aspects to mitigate environmental risks. Ultimately, this research proposes non-cognitive approaches to enhancing synthetic intelligence and outlines future research directions.

Our research involves exploring the thermal behavior of a unique superfluid, comprised of bosonic atoms with linked spin-orbit correlations and neighboring interactions within an optical lattice. The strong spin-orbit coupling creates an irregular spin texture, resulting in finite-momentum states, and our analysis reveals a critical temperature at which the irregular superfluid transitions into a homogeneous state. The temperature at which this phase transition occurs can be controlled through the spin-orbit coupling's strength. The irregular spin texture is stabilized by a critical spin-orbit coupling strength, beyond which it degenerates into the homogeneous state. The combination of spin-fluctuations and regular interactions causes this degeneration. The system's behavior can be mapped onto a well-established model for irregular superfluids, and our analysis reveals a critical temperature at which the irregular superfluid transitions into a re-entrant superfluid state, exhibiting enhanced critical temperatures compared to systems without spin-orbit coupling. The re-entrant phase can be sustained by a critical spin-flux through the regular interactions. The irregular superfluid can transition into the re-entrant superfluid state or the homogeneous state, and the phase diagram can be controlled through the spin-flux through the regular interactions. The irregular superfluid can transition into the re-entrant superfluid state, and the phase diagram can be controlled through the spin-flux through the regular interactions. Consider a finite abelian group $A$ of order $m$, denoted as $\mathbb{Z}_\alpha \times \mathbb{Z}_\beta$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are positive integers. We define specific sets based on the elements of $A$ that have a certain number of generators, and investigate their properties. This leads to various graph representations of $A$, depending on the order of its subgroups, and a key parameter $\lambda$ is introduced to study the properties of these graphs. Specifically, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for these graphs to be perfect, and investigate their independence number and chromatic number in different scenarios.

Recent breakthroughs in AdS/CFT correspondence research have been reviewed, 
focusing primarily on AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ on the D1-D5 boundary. Given the status 
of being the most fully understood sector of the theory, it serves as a 
useful starting point. The discussion will be grounded in low-dimensional 
quantum field theory concepts such as renormalization group, hydrodynamics, 
and supersymmetry. It has been observed that certain aspects of low-dimensional 
theories can be naturally accounted for within the AdS/CFT framework, however 
certain other elements, like chiral symmetry breaking in CFT$_2$, remain 
unresolved. The discussion will also touch on the Type IIA theory's massive 
phase, where time-dependent black hole solutions in AdS$_3$ exist, allowing 
for the creation of a non-equilibrium framework that may address long-standing 
mysteries in AdS/CFT correspondence research.

A Gaussian Process regression model chooses its kernel, a positive definite function, to quantify data noise and interpoint correlations. There's a finite set of elementary expressions, like 1, x^2, x*x, that can be combined to form kernels. We'll take advantage of the fact that Gaussian Process kernels can be stacked and combined to develop new kernels, treating them as functions that take in input data, like (1 + x^2 + x*x)^2. This approach will be applied to a variety of common kernels, like the squared exponential and a kernel that imitates the behavior of a Cauchy process, in order to determine which elementary expressions are the most influential in forming each kernel's structure.

This study investigates the short-term fluctuations in Beam-Induced Neutrals (BIN) emitted by the accelerated beams in a muon collider. Initially, the analysis focuses on a collider employing fully-nested radio-frequency systems with a bunch spacing-to-particle spacing ratio of 1:20, but the observed effects are more broadly applicable. The research reveals that both beam bunches contribute significantly to the BIN power, with the longer period contributing about 60% of the total power. This is an unexpected finding, given the smaller amplitude of the longer period bunch, which is demonstrated through numerical modeling. The study offers two potential reduction strategies for minimizing BIN power. The first approach involves introducing RF errors to modulate the beam charge, effectively averaging the contributions from both bunches and thereby reducing BIN power by a factor of 20. The second method leverages a beam current modulation with a period longer than 4 times the nest length, which is achieved through the interaction between the beam and a external plasma. This modulates the beam charge in a way that maximizes the amplitude of the longer period bunch, thereby significantly decreasing BIN power.

We've proposed a novel technique for introducing differentiable sparseness, effectively determined by a target shape parameter. This method draws upon principles from regularized transportation problems, leveraging Wasserstein distance and Optimal Transport principles. This approach offers several key benefits, notably a nonconvex yet nonnegative gradient, a well-defined optimum, and differentiable sparseness. This method can be effectively used in various settings, notably in neural networks, where it applies universally to matrices. We've thoroughly evaluated our method through numerical experiments, comparing it to existing techniques on both classic problems and neural network applications.

In three-dimensional space, an emergent framework based on the Gross-Pitaevskii equation can be established for describing the non-equilibrium behavior of a weakly interacting Bose gas.  Within the core of the gas's density function, $\sim \Delta \sqrt{\rho(x, t)}$, a specific derivative, $\partial_0 \sqrt{\rho(x, t)}$, can be treated as a constant.  Consequently, the Gross-Pitaevskii equation reduces to a second-order hyperbolic partial differential equation.  Notably, this reduced equation encompasses elements of the Ginzburg-Landau and Dirac equations, as well as the nonlinear Schrodinger equation.  Specifically, in the presence of a potential influenced by multiple variables with a single derivative, it mirrors the Pauli equation, an equation describing semi-conducting materials.  In the absence of potential influences, the equation takes on a form reminiscent of the Dirac equation, an equation describing fermions, as well as the Ginzburg-Landau equation, an equation describing type-II superconductors.  In the scenario where time is treated as the primary variable and spatial dependence is varied, the equation resembles the nonlinear Schrodinger equation, an equation describing nonlinear optics.  This analysis provides a theoretical framework for detecting an emergent Pauli obstruction in the Gross-Pitaevskii formalism.

Software developers widely agree that test smells have a detrimental effect on the quality of test cases and, by extension, the quality of software programs. The impact of test smells on test cases is subjective and depends on the developer's perspective, just like code quality issues. This study aims to gather developers' opinions on the severity of test smells through an online survey, similar to previous studies on code smells, using a standardized questionnaire to measure their views on test smells. The results reveal that most tested code segments are uncomplicated, and few contain complex test smells. Notably, developers' top priorities are reduction and removal of test smells. The study also identifies areas that require improvement in an already established questionnaire, used to measure developers' views on test smells, to ensure it remains effective in future research. The study's findings can inform the development of techniques to address test smells, and their practical implications are presented in the form of recommendations. The study's results can serve as a baseline for future research on the impact of test smells, similar to studies on code smells.

This research explores a nonconvex mathematical framework for modeling complex brush patterns. The proposed model relies on two key components: 1) a nonconvex energy function that minimizes disruptions in the pattern, and 2) an integral term, representing the influence of past brush strokes on current behavior. The goal is to determine optimal brushing sequences over a specified time interval. To address this challenge, we have developed an algorithm combining a type of energy-based minimization and integral term optimization. The effectiveness of this approach has been demonstrated through numerical simulations.

We have developed an event generator, called KKMCee, to simulate the creation of leptons and quarks in particle collisions. This Monte Carlo tool is designed for particle physics research at collider facilities, replacing a previous version called KKMCee. Recent updates in the Code of the Year (2021) version of this event generator have enhanced its capabilities by integrating Monte Carlo data from CTEQ6 parton distribution functions and sixfold polarized simulation features for electron collisions. We have also included functions to account for electron positron pair creation events through various mechanisms such as the two-photon fusion and the weak interaction. To verify the accuracy and performance of this event generator, we performed Monte Carlo simulations for several major particle collisions including the LEP2, ILC, CLIC, CEBAF, JLC, and Future Circular Collider (FCC-ee) experiments.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warning signs for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is challenging due to the signal's noisy and irregular nature. Traditional methods often involve mathematical transformations to regularize the signal, which can introduce artifacts and distort the signal. Instead, we employ a Tiramisu model that leverages deep learning to directly predict IBIs from raw signal data, minimizing distortion and improving accuracy. By comparing our approach with standard methods, we found that it achieves significantly lower errors, with average reductions of 48.2% and 42.1% relative errors in training and testing phases, respectively.

The applicability of the random sample approach, previously successful in matrix applications, has been explored for large-scale tensor processing. In our research, we have developed a more efficient method to calculate the tensor singular value decomposition (TSVDE), requiring significantly fewer passes as well as substantial reductions in both computational and storage costs. The proposed algorithm is compatible with a variety of sampling techniques and can be effectively applied to large-scale problems with limited core memory, ultimately resulting in faster solution times. The performance of our TSVD algorithm has been thoroughly evaluated under various conditions and compared to existing methods.

Real-world networks are frequently represented as dynamic graphs that undergo various changes over time. In this context, embedding evolving graphs involves modeling node attributes in a way that reflects their connections and behavioral patterns over time. This paper offers an extensive review of methods used to represent and attribute nodes in graph modeling, focusing on techniques that account for temporal relationships, such as linking features to past behaviors and incorporating measures of network stability and change. We also explores single-track and multi-track approaches to representing node attributes over time, discussing statistical and machine learning methods that account for temporal dependencies, such as autoregressive models, graph convolutional networks, and influence maximization. Finally, we discuss the challenges and potential future directions of this field.

In light of recent deuterium radioactivity research, a novel approach has been employed to study deuterium's isospin partner, $^7$H, particularly focusing on the 1/2$^+$ isospin-isospin excitation of the 3/2$^+$ deuterium ground state ($^3$H). This analysis involves applying the $^3$H+4n two-body potential, based on the $^3$H ground state, to study $^7$H's spectrum. As a result, the analysis not only accurately reproduces $^7$H's 1/2$^+$ ground state and 7/2$^+$ isospin-degenerate states but also its 1/2$^+$ proton emission decay to alpha particles with a half-life of 2.7 seconds in isolation, matching the 1990 experimental findings without adjusting anything. This was made possible by a recent correction to the Loeb-type $S$-matrix cutoff that prevented unphysical propagating states.

The research investigates ideal contact spheres in 3-dimensional Euclidean space with their second fundamental form conformal. This is equivalent to solving the Nirenberg problem, a complex equation in R^3 that also involves non-linear operator theory and Calabi-Yau equations on the sphere S(2) \R. The investigation focuses on the solution's topological structure, specifically when the solution's singularity cannot be eliminated via a regular transformation, and we demonstrate the existence of such unsolvable singularities.

Deep Learning methods have made significant breakthroughs in unsupervised representation learning. Focusing on clustering problems, previous research highlighted the potential benefits of using neural networks to generate data features. Nevertheless, deep clustering techniques are heavily dependent on parameters such as temperature and cluster numbers, which can be challenging to set. Our work presents a novel method for clustering using neural networks that learns a task-agnostic, distance metric via the Sinkhorn Divergence, ensuring clustering results are invariant to temperature and other parameter settings. Additionally, this approach provides valuable insights into the effect of optimization algorithms on neural network embeddings, specifically for K-Means loss. Lastly, we discuss the theoretical properties of Sinkhorn Divergences in relation to deep clustering problems.

In England, local contact tracing efforts for COVID-19 were augmented by additional staff beyond the core team, but the law enforcement aspect was exclusively handled by public health authorities due to data protection concerns. We aimed to measure the effect of collaborative models on contact tracing efficiency. Our research revealed that areas with more integrated partnerships of contact tracing teams had enhanced performance, as measured by better coverage rates of investigations and more contacts identified. We found similar results when examining the proportion of contacts identified within the specified time frame. Our findings suggested that areas with higher local contact tracing team involvement had lower backlogs in investigations and contacts. Our research indicated that through data sharing, partnership models could enhance the core team's capabilities, resulting in better outcomes.

Accurate 3D spatial mappings of star clusters offer valuable insights into a cluster's development, including its initial formation, age progression, and eventual dissolution. Utilizing the Gaia DR2 stellar database, a 3D spatial mapping of the Melotte 72 star cluster has been created at a distance of approximately 2395 parsecs. The resulting spatial data indicate that Melotte 72 exhibits characteristics of age and composition homogeneity. Analysis of the cluster's spatial distribution in relation to its line of sight reveals that Melotte 72 does not possess any noticeable gaps or irregularities. The cluster's metal content was found to be [Fe/H] = -0.24 with an associated uncertainty, and Melotte 72's total luminosity output was determined to be 1.290 x 10^4 L_solar with an associated error margin. The Gaia DR2 spatial data of Melotte 72 also support a cluster radius of around 16.5 parsecs with an associated error range, and the cluster's overall shape was found to be oblong in nature.

We examine continuous Gaussian processes on the interval $[0,1]^d$ and find that for large $d$, their Betti numbers exhibit linear growth in proportion to $d$. However, in the context of sparse data, we also find that these Betti numbers show a different behavior under dimensionality reduction, where they can change by at most $2$ even when the data dimensions change by $1$. To achieve this, we first establish that the homology groups of these processes converge in some sense to those of a specific Poisson process. Next, we use statistical tools to bound the magnitude of errors in that convergence. Our findings are then applied to the analysis of submanifolds in the context of sparse regression.

Adjusting an eye-in-hand camera is a fundamental challenge in robotics, with the conventional approach relying on external visual markers or prior experience. However, these methods are impractical outside controlled environments. Our novel technique employs an end-to-end network to calculate eye-in-hand camera pose directly from a single RGB image, utilizing an existing 3D mesh model of the robot hand. Our proposed framework is a self-supervised model that trains without ground truth data by simulating adjustments and pose calculations within a digital environment. When applied to real-world scenarios, it outperforms other hand-crafted methods and works effectively without external calibrations or markers, with the results of our model available open-source for widespread use.

In reversal learning, the objective is to discover a hidden reward function within a predetermined set of reward signals, using data obtained by interacting with a system. The key distinction between reversal learning and conventional reinforcement learning is that reward functions are initially unknown and can only be inferred through trial and error. The known reward signals are derived from an unknown original function. The existing body of work in reinforcement learning, which is grounded in dynamic programming, is not directly applicable to this task. The paper investigates the use of constrained reinforcement learning within the context of reversal learning, and provides theoretical bounds on the accuracy of learned functions. The learned functions are found to be close approximations to the underlying reward function, and are within a specified margin of optimality. The paper also presents an empirical application in the context of autonomous mobility, and discusses additional potential uses in various fields such as healthcare and social welfare. The proposed approach is evaluated using data from an autonomous system, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in learning reward functions that closely align with actual user preferences. The learned functions also show a strong correlation with the underlying user preferences, and the authors discuss avenues for further research in future research directions.

The European Space Agency's GAIA mission, a core programme of its science division, was launched in 2013 with the goal of creating a detailed 3D map of the Milky Way, capturing the essence of our Galaxy like never before. By accurately measuring the positions, movements, and velocities of over 1 billion celestial sources, including stars, galaxies, and other astrophysical objects, GAIA will significantly advance our understanding of the Universe. This article provides an overview of the mission, outlining its objectives, design, and operation, before describing the initial science results and their implications on astrophysical knowledge. Finally, a glimpse of the expected scientific outcomes and future observations in the prorgramme's second phase are shared.

The treewidth of a graph is a crucial parameter that facilitates a range of algorithms with guaranteed polynomial time complexity. The treewidth can be calculated as the minimum width of a specific tree representation of the graph's vertices. The task of identifying the optimal treewidth representation is an NP-hard problem; however, algorithms exist that produce approximate solutions with guaranteed polynomial time complexity. The treewidth approximation algorithms can be categorized into two types: vertex approximation and edge approximation. Vertex approximation algorithms aim to reduce the overall number of vertices in the treewidth representation, whereas edge approximation algorithms strive to minimize the number of edges. Our study presents a new vertex approximation algorithm that achieves a guaranteed parameterization of the treewidth with linear time complexity. The proposed algorithm is based on the concept of vertex dividers; our method identifies a specific subset of vertices that can be removed from the graph to ensure a guaranteed treewidth bound with reduced vertices. The algorithm starts with an initial tree representation and iteratively applies two operations: vertex elimination and vertex merging. The process continues until a specific stopping criterion is met to ensure a vertex-bounded treewidth representation. The first operation removes a vertex from the treewidth representation, whereas the second operation integrates the effects of the removed vertex on its neighbors. The algorithm is parameterized by a specific value; when this value is set to 1, it reduces to a previously existing vertex approximation algorithm. The proposed algorithm is experimentally evaluated and demonstrates superior performance in reducing vertices compared to alternative approaches on the benchmark dataset

Current network measures are often based on weighted strength and local clustering properties, but they fail to account for other important aspects of weighted networks, particularly their directed properties. To address this, we have developed a new family of measures that utilize weighted edges to analyze these directed properties. This family of measures includes multiple interpretations, which can be categorized into three types: heterogeneous, inferred, and measured networks. To establish a universal toolbox for weighted edge analysis, we have systematically explored the necessary measures to distinguish between these category groups. Through this research, we have identified and categorize existing measures that were already part of the toolbox, as well as introducing five new measures to fulfill the gaps in the heterogeneous category. This research provides a comprehensive foundation for the weighted edge analysis of directed networks, which is highly relevant for the study of infrastructure, social, and biological systems.

Machine learning has become an integral part of the scientific research landscape, particularly with the emergence of physics-informed neural networks. These networks incorporate known physical principles and laws to optimize their training, often resulting in higher predictive accuracy and improved robustness. A novel approach is presented for estimating the uncertainty in physics-informed neural networks. This method, developed using Bayesian inference, allows for accurate prediction of future data points without the need for resimulation. Utilizing a Gaussian process approximation, the analysis demonstrates that sufficient training data can lead to confident predictions. Furthermore, the framework can be utilized to assess the reliability of predictions made by physics-informed neural networks. Through Monte Carlo sampling, the method demonstrates the potential for significant prediction error at various stages of training, highlighting the significance of post-training evaluation.

Epidemiologic studies heavily rely on air quality models to establish associations between air pollution and health effects, making the interpretation of study results highly dependent on the quality of these models. This presentation will cover the different types of air quality models, evaluating their strengths and limitations in terms of accuracy, reliability, and applicability. The presentation will also explore the challenges posed by spatial and temporal variability in air pollution, particularly with regard to particulate matter and ozone. Furthermore, the presentation will delve into recent advancements in predictive technology, such as machine learning, and their potential applications in air quality models, ultimately setting the stage for future directions in the field.

A Majorana spectrum mimicked by an unconventional spectrum due to Ohmic dissipation can be distinguished by analyzing the normal modes resulting from the Coulomb interaction within a vortices-based system.  Utilizing a non-linear conductance analysis under varying gate voltances, the distinct normal modes associated with the Majorana and dissipation-induced spectra can be pinpointed.  Notably, the Majorana normal mode is characterized by a non-linear Coulomb diamond structure, whereas the dissipation-induced spectrum features linear Coulomb diamonds.  By positioning the Fermi energy at the midpoint of the Coulomb diamond, the systematic suppression of tunneling spectra width can be evaluated against gate voltage variations, thereby directly revealing the presence of a Majorana spectrum.  Furthermore, the proposed method is versatile and can be adapted for use in different Coulomb effective masses, including those resulting from normal tunneling, gapped tunneling, and superconducting tunneling.

Theoretical analysis of linear bandits typically assumes that action sets are finite and discrete. In contrast, contemporary research focuses on sets that are rich, non-discrete, and even continuous. This paper explores linear bandits with continuous action sets and presents two novel estimators for the parameterized kernel matrix that are respectively suitable for finite and infinite action sets. It then establishes the conditions required for the parametric, non-parametric, and empirical risk minimizers to be consistent in this context. The findings indicate that action set richness influences the rate at which these estimators converge. The proposed estimators are evaluated empirically and outperform existing competitors. The results also highlight the importance of considering the bandit scenario when assessing the estimators' consistency.

Graphene with gaps has been a focal point of interest due to the unique combination of chiral spin-polarized edge states and charge neutrality, which makes it suitable for applications in devices that utilize charge and spin properties. Although this material does not exhibit valley Hall effect, due to the absence of distinct energy levels for its two valleys, its properties make it a candidate for another phenomenon, the orbital Hall effect. In this study, we have shown that in gapped graphene, an external magnetic field creates orbital Hall currents, which arise from the differences in edge state energies caused by the magnetic field. Our findings indicate that this effect does not depend on the specific type of edge state (edge or ribbon) and do not experience a resistance drop in the orbital Hall effect, unlike the case for the orbital spin Hall effect.

Machine learning models' effectiveness can be compromised by data corruption. 
This study focuses on graph data contamination and proposes a new method for detecting and mitigating it within neural networks. 
Since current approaches are problem-specific and don't generalise well, we've developed a more adaptable solution utilizing reinforcement learning. 
By applying reinforcement learning to graph manipulation, we've created an innovative method that graph data to enhance model resilience. 
Through experiments on various graph datasets, we've demonstrated the benefits of our approach over traditional methods.

The process of matching objects between photometric and astrometric catalogues is crucial for various astrophysical applications, particularly at the stage of data reduction. The standard protocol involves using astrometric data to determine expected coordinates, and then comparing them to photometric counterparts from a matched catalogue. The quality of astrometric data significantly affects the accuracy of this process, and therefore, plays a crucial role in matching objects. In this study, a method was developed to improve the astrometric data used in matching objects by leveraging the additional information provided by photometric data. The results showed that, on average, this approach increased the radius of circular astrometric error by 30% for existing photometric data, and reduced discrepancies between catalogues by 20%. The method was applied to real-world data from the Gaia DR2 and the HAWK's Wide Field Camera, and led to a significant improvement of 30% in matching objects from two catalogues.

In this paper, we study the topological properties of infinite hypergraphs and their finite minimal subgraphs. Our main achievement is the proof that for any infinite hypergraph, the family of its finite minimal subgraphs does not satisfy the Higman's Embedding Theorem, which indicates the topological structure of the hypergraph cannot be fully embedded within a finite-dimensional Euclidean space. This result extends to the projective infinite hypergraphs, meaning those obtained by removing a single point from them. Additionally, we investigate the interrelation of our finding with open problems raised by Tchakaloff in 1929 and Kolay in 1982.

Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive conceptual frameworks, which are commonly visualized in diagram form to facilitate navigation, comprehension, and expansion. With thousands of such ontologies now at our disposal, users face difficulties locating and processing individual concepts. To address these challenges, we suggest a novel visualization method, OntoPlot, which is designed to capture large-scale relationships within extensive conceptual frameworks. By integrating three distinct views - an expanded overview and two focused analyses - OntoPlot enables users to gain a deeper understanding of individual concepts within a sub-set of relationships. A prototype of OntoPlot has been implemented and demonstrated using the Gene Ontology, with promising results.

We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss and CycleGAN to exploit unlabeled data in semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. Inter-domain loss facilitates domain adaptation by matching data distributions, whereas CycleGAN induces a cycle-consistent training paradigm. Experimentally, our method surpasses conventional inter-domain loss-based approaches and achieves comparable performance with fully-supervised models on the TIMIT and LibriSpeech datasets.

This study explores the feasibility of deep active prediction methods for autonomous robot navigation. Through simulation-based experiments, we demonstrate that a robot can efficiently navigate by selecting and sampling explicit predictions from a trained generative model, which exhibits superior performance compared to sampling random states and measures its uncertainty using a novel entropy-based approach.

Our research focuses on the Soret effect in systems containing freely rotating molecules, where we examine both the symmetric and asymmetric cases. We model the molecules as a combination of arms and a backbone, and investigate how the molecules' geometry and orientation influence the thermal gradient. Using mean-field approximation, we calculate the contribution of the rotational degree of freedom to the Soret coefficient. We find that this contribution is dependent on the molecules' geometry and the thermal gradient strength. Moreover, the relative position of the arms with respect to the backbone affects the Soret coefficient, leading to changes in the diffusion process.

The capability of transformer-based language models to analyze the grammatical structure of sentences makes them well-suited for evaluating written content. In this study, we examined the performance of four efficient transformer models - HT-R, HR, EMTN (Lite), and ALBERT - on Automated Essay Scoring tasks. Our analysis of their capabilities is based on their ability to understand sentence patterns, predict task difficulty, understand essay content, and detect copying. The results indicate that the HT-R model achieves the highest overall performance across all tasks. Moreover, we found that the performance of these models is correlated with their ability to accurately analyze sentence patterns.

One of the most critical components of advanced driver assistance systems is pedestrian detection. Despite significant advancements in this area, modern deep networks still generate a substantial number of false positives, particularly in real-world scenarios. To overcome this challenge, we develop novel techniques for suppressing false positives and enhancing the recall rate of pedestrian detection. These methods involve re-examining box predictions in an unsupervised manner and can be applied across various domains with minimal additional processing required. Our approach yields impressive results on public datasets, showcasing a notable 52.73% improvement in F1-score. Additionally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in adapting pedestrian models across domains with success rates exceeding standard techniques by 15.2-20.9% and comparable to recent state-of-the-art solutions.

This study presents an innovative method for enhancing low-quality music recordings made on mobile devices, which often suffer from distortion, noise, and surrounding environmental interference capturing poor room characteristics. A novel deep learning technique combines image translation and speaker analysis to revitalize the recordings, drawing inspiration from a system that translates low-pitched voices into high-pitched ones. A training dataset was created by simulating the effects of poor recording equipment and ambient noise to evaluate the method's effectiveness in correcting these issues. Comparisons with established audio enhancement techniques reveal that our approach produces more natural-sounding outcomes with minimal loss of the original audio's distinctive characteristics.

Our primary objective is to comprehensively assess how throwing movements with inaccurate release points affect user perception. To achieve this, we created FauxThrow, a novel throwing simulation system, enabling the seamless integration of virtual objects into realistic throwing sequences. By incorporating user studies with varying release points and target distances, we analyzed perceptions of throwing accuracy, difficulty, and effort. The results indicate that slight deviations in release points lead to considerable variations in user experience. Furthermore, we discovered that decreased throwing accuracy was associated with increased perceived difficulty, while exaggerated effort judgments were observed in cases where release points preceded the throw. The findings of our study stress the significance of accurate release points in the authenticity of throwing movements.

This study presents an innovative NMT system that leverages a tree structured decoding method, combining the efficiency of top-down parsing with the precision of bottom-up machine translation. The proposed approach begins by generating partial sentences and then applies a syntactic linear model to guide the completion of sentences in a top-down manner. Experimental results indicate that this new system can achieve comparable performance to state-of-the-art samples NMT models on two assessment datasets, while demonstrating an impressive speedup of decoding. Notably, an early stop in the decoding process was implemented, resulting in a tree structured translation model that showed strong accuracy, parsing the sentences with impressive accuracy in a majority of cases.

The formation of complex molecules in interstellar clouds is influenced by the stability of their building block associations, known as molecular complexes.  A new platform called the Binding Energy Assessment Platform (BEAP) has been developed to provide information on the stability of these complexes.  Through analysis of quantum chemical binding energy data, molecular rotation-vibration frequency maps are generated, allowing them to be searched based on specific parameters.  A database of astrophysically relevant molecular complexes with accompanying frequency maps is included in the platform.  Frequency maps can be used to determine the reliability of theoretical binding energy models by comparing them to experimental data.  This will help scientists understand the stability of molecular complexes in interstellar clouds.  A tutorial is available online to demonstrate the platform's functionality.

A multiplicative stochastic process that builds upon previous values with random increments is analyzed, along with its correlation properties in a Euclidean space context. It is demonstrated that this process has a lower bound, proportional to the square root of the sample size, multiplied by a time-dependent constant. To illustrate the process's applications, two potential uses are presented: first, as a detection method for comparing two stochastic processes, and second, as a means to predict the ultimate behavior of a stochastic process not yet converged.

In the realm of quantum statistical physics, a significant challenge is to develop an efficient algorithm for calculating the expectation value of multi-qubit terms in the Hamiltonian. This expectation value serves as an optimization criterion in the variational quantum algorithm, which trains a near-optimal quantum state on a noisy quantum computer by using gradient descent. However, conventional methods for calculating expectation values scale poorly with the number of qubits due to the increasing depth required to accurately project a quantum state onto specific basis states. This letter presents an innovative approach called shallow shadows, an efficient expectation assessment protocol that achieves a satisfactory trade-off between circuit depth and accuracy. This depth-sensitive method allows for an optimal balance between the circuit depth used to prepare a term in the Hamiltonian and the accuracy required, while maintaining a linear relationship between both factors. Furthermore, shallow shadows has been theoretically demonstrated to meet the requirements of the QALG2 standard, which is a widely accepted benchmark for quantum algorithms. This depth-sensitive method is ideal for noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers, which are particularly limited by circuit depth at their current stage. This depth-sensitive method is also suitable for classical computers, which face scalability issues. This depth-sensitive approach has been theoretically demonstrated to meet the requirements of the QALG2 standard, which is a benchmark for quantum algorithms.

The researchers in this study, C. S. Adler and M. J. Lutzhein, examined the properties of solutions to the Davey-Stewartson II equations using a Riemann-Hilbert framework. They found that the solutions' associated jump relations exhibit unusual behavior near singular points. Notably, along the line y=-x, the solutions' behavior becomes increasingly complex as the wavenumber k approaches infinity, transitioning from a first-order non-linear effect to a second-order linear effect. This transition occurs due to the collapse of an infinite strip under the soliton backflow map into the interval between two solitons.

Recent text classification advancements, exemplified by the state-of-the-art Sibyl system, primarily focus on achieving high accuracy. Consequently, this area of study has been relatively underexplored in the context of text classification. As the use of machine learning increases in critical applications like security clearance, medical diagnosis, and law, the need for more reliable systems, immune to potential attacks on classification models, grows. In this study, we introduce the concept of sibylvariant modifications. These modifications enhance the stability of text classification models by identifying and stabilizing inconsistent training data influences. Our research reveals that applying sibylvariant modifications to a well-established text classification dataset can improve robustness and accuracy, and can potentially be combined with other classification methods to augment the performance of machine learning models in text classification.

In the realm of limited data, a new interest has emerged in finding representations that enable tasks to be learned independently with minimal common examples between them. A representation is considered'meta' if it effectively leverages a small set of shared training data to transfer knowledge across tasks. However, a lack of common data does not necessarily imply a meta representation can be learned, as we have found that current algorithms are not capable of achieving this goal. Our work focuses on developing a new class of algorithms designed to learn a meta-linear representation even when there is no shared data across tasks. A 'demonstrable' meta-learning algorithm is one in which the learned representation is understandable and analyzable. Our objective is a representation that minimizes the worst-case risk over a set of tasks with potentially random data. A new category of simple, linear representations has been developed, along with corresponding 'demonstrable' meta-learning algorithms. These algorithms have been theoretically proven to meet an upper limit on performance when enough training data is available, while also providing an optimal Lower Bound on performance when training data is scarce. Importantly, our findings show that even with an infinite amount of data, a 'demonstrable' meta-learning algorithm is unable to achieve the optimal performance, highlighting significant drawbacks of existing methods.

In machine translation, knowledge distillation has proven to be an effective technique for creating compact models that match the performance of larger models, especially in settings where data is scarce. Another promising approach for model compression is quantization, which can significantly reduce a model's memory footprint. While quantization and distillation share some similarities, particularly in terms of adapting to scarce resources, there has been little research examining their relative robustness in low-resource contexts. This paper investigates the stability of these compression methods, particularly in contexts where the training dataset is limited, using a Monte-Carlo approach to test the performance variability associated with each method. Our findings suggest that, compared to distillation, quantization is prone to greater performance instability, particularly in contexts where the dataset is extremely limited. However, when the training dataset is extensive, both methods are able to produce high-quality translations that are comparable in terms of BLEU score.

A general expression for the Lagrangian density of a single hypergraph is developed, with the condition that interactions solely occur between nearest neighbor hyperedges. Results show that for certain values of Lagrangian parameters, the free energy exhibits a complex relationship with temperature, displayable in a phase diagram. Findings indicate that ground states of the system transform at a critical temperature, characterized by an entropy of unlimited growth, signifying the presence of a critical point. We further demonstrate the existence of a second-order phase transition at a critical point, marked by a discontinuity in the order parameter. The study of single hypergraph thermodynamics is initiated, with a specific case explored.

Deep learning-based diagnostic systems have shown great success in medical imaging. However, these networks typically demand substantial quantities of labeled data to function effectively. To develop reliable medical image analysis systems with minimal labeled data requirements, it's essential to incorporate data enhancement techniques. This work investigates how image augmentation methods, specifically for pneumonia segmentation, affect model performance when trained with different amounts of labeled data. We also examine the influence of various combination techniques of individual augmentation methods on model performance. Our experiments using a ResNet50 architecture on CT scan images revealed that a combination of rotation and depth transfer resulted in the best model performance when trained with limited labeled data.

Capable image description generation is a complex task requiring not only advanced image understanding abilities but also sophisticated language management as well. While data-driven approaches have been widely adopted in this field, they often rely on the flexibility of neural networks to adapt to various tasks. This paper introduces a novel paradigm, Neural Prompting, which enables efficient task control by incorporating external, reusable text prompts. We explore the feasibility of adapting Neural Prompting for image description tasks and develop innovative strategies, including the optimization of baseline models, custom prompt design, and optimization regularization. Our experiments demonstrate that Neural Prompting can successfully describe images, yielding significant improvements in description quality, particularly in aspects such as coherence, relevance, and details, with improvements of 4.08, 2.23, and 2.93, respectively, in metrics-based evaluation.

This paper delves into the concept of harm, often seen as the opposite of benefit, and its various causal aspects. In everyday language, statements about harm are typically based on consequences, for example, "Smoking will harm your health." In contrast, professionals, including ethicists and decision analysts, discuss harm in terms of contributions, drawing on concepts from causal diagrams and structural causal models. This paper aims to bridge this gap by clearly defining harm in terms of consequences within a comprehensive framework known as cumulative causality, which integrates concepts from cumulative structural causal models and causal networks. This paper also discusses how to utilize this definition for in-depth causal analysis, focusing on two key aspects: identifying the causal factors that contribute to a phenomenon's severity and developing strategies to mitigate a problem's impact.

This study demonstrates the potential of MMLSpark, an open-source library, in streamlining deep learning workflows. We highlight its practical applications in various contexts, particularly in scaling up machine learning tasks and integrating data preprocessing steps. By combining MMLSpark and the open-source deep learning framework Microsoft Cognitive Toolkit (CTK), known today as Azure Machine Learning (AML), this paper shows how these tools can streamline a complete machine learning workflow.

Recent advancements in end-to-end speech translation have been notable, yet speech translation to languages with limited data remains a significant challenge. A key hurdle is the lack of large-scale, high-quality training data in such languages. Zero-shot speech translation, which relies on a multilingual translation model, presents a viable solution, but existing approaches focus primarily on text-to-text translation. When it comes to zero-shot speech translation, the need to first generate text in an intermediate language with ample text data creates a significant obstacle. To overcome this, we develop a novel approach for zero-shot speech translation that employs a two-stage model. A pre-trained speech-synthesis model is used to generate speech from intermediate text, which is derived through translation facilitated by a pre-trained translation model. We evaluate our proposed approach in various scenarios and find that it outperforms previous methods.

This work introduces a novel extension of the classical heat diffusion model, incorporating memories within the boundary constraints as described by Coleman and Gurtin. The investigation seeks to clarify the dynamic behavior of a solid structure subject to thermal gradients across its boundary, which undergoes changes in boundary conditions influenced by time-varying temperatures. The resulting system of equations is analyzed within a bounded area $\Omega \times [0, +\infty)$, utilizing functional spaces to derive well-posedness results for the associated boundary value problem. Lastly, a comprehensive study is provided through the construction of a semigroup, which in turn allows for the establishment of long-term dynamics, as well as various asymptotic outcomes.

Precise and detailed load forecasts are vital for efficient low-voltage network management, requiring a higher time resolution to achieve this. However, existing load forecasting methods often compromise on accuracy or detail due to the limitations of available data. This study investigates the use of high-resolution load data combined with long-term historical data, and explores the potential benefits of forecast fusion for predicting low-voltage network load profiles. To address the challenge of varying data availability, the study employs probabilistic forecasting, enabling the calculation of prediction intervals based on historical data and update rules. The performance of forecast fusion methods is evaluated using statistical metrics, and the calculated prediction intervals are validated against empirical distributions from distribution system operators. The results indicate significant potential in applying forecast fusion techniques for daily peak load predictions, and the study contributes methodologically to the field of load forecasting, particularly for low-voltage networks, and provides insights for grid operators on how to utilize forecast fusion for load predictions, ultimately leading to more accurate prediction intervals.

Domain knowledge integration is a critical phase of machine learning model development, 
requiring unique consideration at each model stage from data preparation to evaluation.
This paper synthesizes comprehensive research into a thorough, structured guide 
for incorporating domain knowledge into machine learning models. We examine the 
effect of domain knowledge integration on data preprocessing and feature selection 
and retention, as well as models and model assessments. Additionally, we discuss 
the computational methodologies supporting the evaluation of machine learning models.

The current machine learning methods for COVID-19 detection rely heavily on annotations containing specific object labels, which are scarce and becoming increasingly expensive. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a new framework based on weakly supervised learning to detect COVID-19 without relying on expensive, fully annotated data sets. By using image-level labels, our method can identify latent object labels in the data, allowing it to perform lesion localization and segmentation. We develop a new approach that uses latent object labels to perform semantic segmentation, using a technique that preserves instance boundaries. By applying a new model, our experiments show significant improvements in detection accuracy, with results comparable to methods using precise object labels in three different datasets. Additionally, we found that our method successfully localized and segmented COVID-19 lesions in Chest X-Ray images, with an accuracy of 71.38% +/- 7.23% in a large-scale evaluation.

A novel, automated method for vertebrae localization and identification in CT scans is introduced, primarily focusing on the spine. This method is designed to be flexible and adaptable to a range of spinal curvatures and pathological postures. The approach involves initially rectifying the spine in 3D, followed by a optimization technique that takes into account anatomical constraints to identify the vertebrae. The method is trained using an extensive dataset of 3D spine images, containing diverse spinal curvatures and pathologies, to establish a prior understanding of vertebrae configurations. By combining this information with input image data, the optimization algorithm generates an optimal solution. The method is complemented by a technique that utilizes a Gaussian distribution to propagate uncertainty and errors, allowing for accurate vertebrae localization. Evaluations using a large, diverse dataset have demonstrated the method's high accuracy and robustness in identifying vertebrae across a range of spinal curvatures and pathologies.

Dynamics and electron-impact cross sections for scattering on  rare gas atoms will be examined when atoms are enclosed in a cavity and subjected to a short pulse of infrared light. This will explore how the interaction between atoms and the cavity affects the distribution of energy, particularly the development of a long-range attractive potential, affecting cross sections in a manner that extends beyond the conventional forward and reverse scattering framework. This research will be carried out using the final-state interaction approach, incorporating the effects of atomic polarization and the constraints imposed by the cavity. It is found that cross sections exhibit enhancements of up to 10-fold compared to non-cavity conditions, with favorable orientations of the infrared field, due to the formation of a metastable state with enhanced long-range attractive properties, caused by the transfer of energy via vacuum fluctuations. This metastable state can persist for a significant period, several hundred femtoseconds, due to the influence of the cavity. This effect is found to be associated with the formation of a long-range attractive potential with a minimum point close to the atom. This results in an enhanced cross section for forward scattering by several orders of magnitude. This can be understood by the application of the Bohr van der Waals model, modified to account for the effects of the cavity. This research will be compared with experimental results from non-resonant scattering, highlighting the effects of the cavity on this process through the formation of a similar metastable state. This will be contrasted with the case of resonant scattering

In contrast to traditional actuators with fixed characteristics, elastic actuators wield the ability to adapt their mechanical properties in response to diverse stimuli, allowing them to address a wide range of actuators. This research focuses on the role of elastic actuators within quadruped locomotion, an application in which they can counteract drawbacks associated with conventional actuators. An elastic actuator model is developed, which enables the simulation tool AIMS to model the dynamic relationship between the elastic actuator's physical properties and its influence on the robot's motion. Building on this relationship, reinforcement learning is employed to optimize quadruped locomotion when utilizing elastic actuators. The results indicate that the quadruped can move at increased speed and greater trajectory deviation when utilizing elastic actuators compared to traditional actuators, while maintaining a comparable energy consumption. Additionally, the findings show that the dynamic range of the elastic actuator can be further enhanced by fine-tuning its policy.

The study of quantum separability has significant implications for quantum cryptography and quantum information theory. We introduce a new approach based on a variational method to determine the separability of quantum states. This approach provides insight into the non-linear decomposition of quantum operators. In addition, we outline potential applications of this method to investigate the non-linear spectrum shift phenomenon.

A specific instability in the Edge Plasma, known as the small-scale ripple mode, can occur in collisionless slabs near the Edge of a plasma. This ripples tend to appear along the magnetic field lines and can cause the plasma to undulate in a wave-like fashion. Researchers have studied ripples through computer simulations and have found that they have a characteristic size that is determined by the balance between certain physical forces. This ripples can cause the plasma to lose stability as they grow, leading to ripples that penetrate deeper into the plasma. This can cause the plasma to lose its balance and lead to a loss of energy. This process can play a role in a phenomenon known as "ripening of the magnetosphere" where the plasma loses its balance and leads to a loss of energy.

Recent breakthroughs in image editing technology have generated considerable interest across various sectors, with personalization being a key application. This study explores a more sophisticated approach to personalized search in the realm of fashion, where images are retrieved based on style. We propose an innovative method for semi-supervised feature-level editing of fashion images, allowing similar items to be optimized in terms of fashion trends and ultimately improved for retrieval purposes. We demonstrate that our technique yields high-quality results, is efficient to scale, and effectively enhances personalized search in the fashion sector, particularly when utilized with state-of-the-art retrieval methods.

The deep learning technique holds significant potential for solving various inverse problems arising in imaging, such as deblurring, denoising, and reconstruction tasks. In our research, we leverage the dual gradient method to address linear problems within Banach spaces, focusing on the application of neural networks that output vectors from Banach spaces. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates the convergence of the proposed approach under standard assumptions. Our experiments validate the effectiveness of the dual gradient method in both synthetic and real-world scenarios, particularly for a denoising task involving neural networks that produce positive values.

Determining the depth of a scene from light field images is a complex computational task requiring high processing power due to the massive data required, amounting to 4n^2 pixels per scene depth. The standard approach to achieve real-time depth estimation involves assigning a cost to each sample in the 4D light field image, with the cost determined by scene depth. However, this conventional method is inefficient as it fails to account for occlusion, resulting in significant distortions in the disoccluded regions. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel cost builder that is aware of occlusions, enabling efficient utilization of sparse data, such as slits of aperture, to derive full 4D light field images. The proposed method is designed to maintain sparse data integrity, with our occlusion-aware cost builder accurately capturing epipolar geometry and sparse occlusions, thereby outperforming conventional methods. The proposed method has been validated on public datasets, with results showing disocclusion-free depth estimates, yielding superior outcomes on public datasets.

This study uses the bilinear method to derive consistent Fokas-Lenells equations from the Jimbo-Miwa type linear system associated with the Fokas-Lenells equations, resulting in multiple consistent systems of partial differential equations.

The action of gravity is a key component that describes how matter interacts with the gravitational field. However, traditional actions based on general relativity fall short in explaining phenomena that go beyond Riemannian geometry. A more effective approach can be found in double field theory (DFT), a framework that allows for the description of non-associative, non-commutative geometry. By drawing on DFT's capabilities, we have developed an alternative gravitational action that incorporates non-metricity and non-metricity-like terms, similar to what is seen in theories of torsion. These terms have significant effects on how gravity behaves at the boundaries of space and time. Our new action also ensures that a boundary version of the holographic Weyl anomaly remains valid, thus confirming a long-standing hypothesis regarding the anomaly's structure.

The widespread adoption of wireless networks in homes has led to the emergence of a dense network of Access Points. To improve network performance, using multiple Access Points with different frequency bands is beneficial. However, this causes interference between them, affecting the performance of other devices. To mitigate these issues, using IEEE 802.11k/v standards allows for the management of network architecture and optimal device selection. This paper explores the use of these standards to develop a device selection mechanism that takes into account the capabilities of each device and the performance of the network. By leveraging these standards, our mechanism ensures minimal interference and optimal coexistence, resulting in a stable network. Through simulation, we demonstrate that our mechanism outperforms existing methods by 25% in terms of network performance.
